case_study_insert.main_stem: Zephyr & Loom Fabrics (ZLF) is a partnership in the sustainable home-textile and fashion-fabric e-commerce sector, employing a workforce of 34. Founded in 2018 by partners Priya Loomis and Daniel Zephyr in Copenhagen, the business sells dyed fabrics online to craft and fashion makers through its own website and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. ZLF plans to invest $540,000 in a digital fabric-printing and online fulfilment hub, financed by a $320,000 bank loan and $220,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $21.00, and sells 36,000 units a year. ZLF faces two operational problems: dye waste has reached 6.8% and customer deliveries are running late.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q4 2026: Dye waste ran at 6.8% of materials, down from 8.3%, and 27 fabric rolls were rejected for colour inconsistency out of 1,500 inspected. Customer returns were 310 units and 38 complaints concerned late delivery. Average order dispatch time was 6.2 days against a 4-day promise. A survey of 350 makers found 64% would pay $1.50 more for digitally printed fabric and 57% value faster delivery. Retraining a dye technician costs $520; a computer colour-matching system costs $28,000.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Zephyr & Loom Fabrics as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (January 2027): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 5.0% to 5.75%, increasing borrowing costs on the $320,000 loan. (2) The national minimum wage will increase 5.5% from $12.71 to $13.40 an hour from April 2027, raising wage costs for the 34 staff. (3) Dye and chemical input costs have risen 12.8% year-on-year, while consumer spending on home textiles grew 2.6% in the same period.

questions.question_text: ZLF plans to fund its $540,000 digital fabric-printing hub with a $320,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for ZLF of using $220,000 retained profit instead of borrowing more.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using $220,000 of retained profit reduces the amount borrowed and avoids interest and capital repayments on that portion, protecting cash flow alongside fixed costs of $240,000 a year. The saving can be spent on the $28,000 colour-matching system or on tackling the 6.8% dye waste, rather than paid to a lender, and the $21.00 selling price need not rise to cover extra finance costs.

Point 2: Retained profit has no security or repossession risk, so the printing and fulfilment hub is safe even if demand from craft makers disappoints. It also protects the partners' control of the business: no bank can impose conditions on how the website or printing is run, which suits the flat structure and laissez-faire leadership. Committing $220,000 of profit signals confidence to suppliers while the partnership negotiates around 12.8% dye-cost inflation and 38 complaints about late delivery. Avoiding extra borrowing also leaves room to fund the $28,000 colour-matching system if the 6.8% dye waste fails to fall, without returning to the bank.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to ZLF's funding decision and expansion.

questions.question_text: ZLF is launching its digitally printed fabrics. Consider craft trade fairs, social media video advertising, or email marketing to existing makers. Which should ZLF choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Craft trade fairs: Fairs let makers see and touch printed fabric, which builds trust and can generate immediate orders for a Copenhagen-based partnership. Staff can explain the sustainable printing process directly. However, stands, travel and staff time are costly for a workforce of 34, and the audience is geographically limited, so fairs cannot easily deliver the 36,000 units a year needed to justify the $540,000 hub.

Social media video advertising: Video can show colour and print quality online, which matters because 64% of surveyed makers would pay $1.50 more for digitally printed fabric and 57% value faster delivery. Platforms allow precise targeting of craft and fashion audiences and can link straight to the website, with measurable spend within the $540,000 budget. The drawbacks are crowded feeds, rising costs and the need for regular new creative content.

Email marketing to existing makers: This is cheap, fast and uses the customer list ZLF already has, so it can announce the launch at almost no extra cost and encourage repeat orders. It is measurable and easy to tailor. Its weakness is reach: it cannot attract new makers, and if the 38 late-delivery complaints are not resolved, repeated emails may annoy existing customers rather than win sales.

Recommendation: ZLF should choose social media video advertising, supported by a low-cost email announcement to existing makers. Video reaches new customers nationally and demonstrates the printed fabric that 64% of makers value, while email cannot grow the customer base; trade fairs are rejected as expensive and too local for a business selling mainly through its website. A small fair presence can be reconsidered once the 6.8% dye waste and delivery times are under control.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of ZLF with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of ZLF with a well-justified recommendation explaining why trade fairs and email-only marketing lose.

questions.question_text: ZLF's dye waste is 6.8% and 38 customers complained about late delivery. Explain two benefits for ZLF of its laissez-faire leadership style in a flat structure.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership lets the experienced dye technicians decide how to reduce the 6.8% waste themselves, using their practical knowledge of the vats. Because the flat structure has few managerial layers, a technician can adjust a dye run without waiting for Priya Loomis or Daniel Zephyr, which matters when 27 rolls out of 1,500 were rejected for colour inconsistency and the earlier waste figure was 8.3%.

Point 2: Delegation can speed up responses to the 38 late-delivery complaints and the 6.2-day dispatch time against a 4-day promise, because the workforce of 34 closest to dispatch can rearrange work without seeking approval. Autonomy may raise job satisfaction and reduce the risk of mistakes in a business with fixed costs of $240,000 a year and a $540,000 investment. The partners keep overall control of the $28,000 colour-matching purchase, so freedom operates within agreed limits rather than becoming a lack of direction.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to ZLF's waste, complaints and structure.

questions.question_text: ZLF wants to reduce the 27 rejected fabric rolls and its 6.8% dye waste. Consider retraining a dye technician in colour control or buying a computer colour-matching system. Which should ZLF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Retraining a dye technician: At $520 per person this is cheap beside the $540,000 printing hub, and it improves the skill of the workforce of 34 so that colour mistakes are spotted during dyeing. Given that waste has fallen from 8.3% to 6.8% and 27 of 1,500 rolls were rejected, better judgement at the vat could push the figure lower and make good use of laissez-faire leadership. The limit is that human consistency varies, and training one technician does not help when other staff run the machines.

Computer colour-matching system: Costing $28,000, this gives repeatable recipes and should attack the root cause of colour inconsistency across all shifts, cutting the 27 rejected rolls and supporting the premium that 64% of makers would pay. It also reduces dependence on individual skill and helps meet the 4-day dispatch promise by avoiding re-dyeing. Against this, $28,000 is a larger one-off outlay, staff need training to use it, and it will not solve the 38 late-delivery complaints that arise after dyeing.

Decision: ZLF should buy the computer colour-matching system and fund technician refresher training alongside it. The $28,000 cost is small relative to fixed costs of $240,000 and the $540,000 hub, and it gives consistent results across the whole workforce, so retraining alone is rejected as too dependent on one person and unlikely to eliminate all 27 rejects. The $520 training places should still be kept so staff can operate the system confidently, combining technology with skills rather than choosing only one. They should set a target for the 27 rejected rolls and review the 6.8% waste monthly, so the $28,000 spend is judged against the 12.8% rise in dye costs.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two quality options with limited application to ZLF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both options in the context of ZLF.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of ZLF with a well-justified decision covering cost, consistency and waste reduction.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how ZLF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $240,000 ÷ ($21.00 − $9.00) = $240,000 ÷ $12.00 = 20,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 20,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $21.00 − $9.00 = $12.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $12.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways ZLF's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Break-even output of 20,000 units against sales of 36,000 units leaves a margin of safety of 16,000 units, so the partners can see how far demand from makers could fall before the $540,000 hub becomes unprofitable.
2. Contribution per unit of $12.00 helps test the $1.50 premium that 64% of makers would accept: raising price to $22.50 would lift contribution to $13.50 and speed repayment of the $320,000 bank loan.
3. The 20,000-unit break-even figure sets a sales floor for servicing the $320,000 loan and for deciding whether the $28,000 colour-matching system is affordable from contribution above break-even.
4. Unit cost of $15.67 ($240,000 ÷ 36,000 units = $6.67 plus $9.00 variable cost) gives a monthly benchmark to track the 6.8% dye waste and the 6.2-day dispatch time against the 4-day promise.

questions.model_answer: (i) break-even output = 20,000 units | (ii) contribution per unit = $12.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 16,000 units against 36,000-unit sales; testing the $1.50 premium on $12.00 contribution; servicing the $320,000 bank loan; unit cost of $15.67 to monitor 6.8% dye waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate ZLF's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has ZLF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.30 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.40 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.70 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.90 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $90,000 + $75,000 + $30,000 = $195,000; 2025 current assets = $70,000 + $90,000 + $36,000 = $196,000. Dividing by current liabilities of $150,000 in 2024 and $140,000 in 2025 gives the first pair of figures. Removing stock leaves $105,000 in 2024 and $126,000 in 2025, and dividing those by the same liabilities gives the second pair.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved. The first ratio rose from 1.30 to 1.40 because current liabilities fell from $150,000 to $140,000 while current assets edged up, giving more cover for the $540,000 printing hub commitments. The second ratio improved from 0.70 to 0.90, so ZLF relies less on selling its $70,000 of inventories to pay short-term debts, which is helpful when 6.8% dye waste and 27 rejected rolls can make stock harder to sell. However, trade receivables rose from $75,000 to $90,000 and cash from $30,000 to $36,000 only slightly, so much cash is tied up in customers; the $320,000 bank loan also brings interest obligations if rates rise.

Conclusion: ZLF's financial position has improved. Both measures are higher and the rise in the second measure shows the gain is not merely stock-driven. The residual risk is slower collection from makers, so the partners should tighten credit control before committing more of the $540,000 investment while 38 delivery complaints remain unresolved.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether ZLF's position improved.

questions.question_text: ZLF is considering a $1.50 premium for digitally printed fabric. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for ZLF of this decision.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 350 makers shows 64% would pay $1.50 more for digitally printed fabric and 57% value faster delivery, so the premium is evidence-based and would raise contribution per unit from $12.00 to $13.50. Across 36,000 units that is $54,000 a year (36,000 × $1.50), helping ZLF cover fixed costs of $240,000 and part of the $540,000 hub cost even with home-textile spending up only 2.6%.

Disadvantage: The 36% of makers who would not pay more may switch to plain fabric, and the 12.8% rise in dye and chemical input costs could absorb much of the $1.50 before it reaches profit. With dye waste at 6.8%, 27 rejected rolls and 38 late-delivery complaints, a higher price may raise expectations that ZLF currently struggles to meet. The partners should therefore trial the premium on one print range while checking that the $28,000 colour-matching system reduces rejects. They should compare orders from the 64% who welcome printing with the 36% who do not, so the premium does not hasten a fall in demand for plain dyed fabric.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to ZLF's survey, costs and quality record.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 12.8% rise in dye and chemical input costs will affect ZLF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.0% to 5.75%): On the specified $320,000 bank loan, if the rate is variable the extra interest is 0.75% of $320,000 = $2,400 a year (0.0075 × $320,000). That is small beside fixed costs of $240,000 a year and can be removed by fixing the rate, so this is the least significant of the three changes; higher rates could still dampen the 2.6% growth in home-textile spending.

Minimum wage rise (5.5%, to $13.40 an hour): The insert gives 34 staff but no hours worked or pay rates, so an annual wage bill cannot be invented. Qualitatively the rise increases the cost of dispatching orders and cannot be avoided. Its effect depends on the 36,000 units sold and on whether laissez-faire leadership maintains productivity; with 38 delivery complaints and a 6.2-day dispatch time, extra wage costs may not translate into better service unless the 4-day promise is met more often.

Dye and chemical inflation (12.8%): The insert gives a $9.00 variable cost per unit but does not decompose it. The honest upper bound is 0.128 × $9.00 = $1.152 per unit, which over 36,000 units is $41,472 a year (36,000 × $1.152). Even a smaller increase reduces the $12.00 contribution on every metre sold, and the 6.8% dye waste makes the problem worse because material is already being lost before it becomes a sale.

Conclusion: The 12.8% rise in dye and chemical costs will have the greatest impact. It can add about $41,472 a year, far above the $2,400 interest change, and it can be bounded from the insert whereas the wage rise cannot be quantified. Unlike the interest rise, it cannot be eliminated by fixing a rate and it strikes every unit of the 36,000 sold. ZLF should renegotiate dye supply, use the $28,000 colour-matching system to cut the 27 rejected rolls, and trial the $1.50 premium to recover part of the increase.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to ZLF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on ZLF's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of ZLF with a well-justified judgement that dye cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
